t: How a controller thinks: the scan and the rung
html:
A relay panel is wired; a controller is scanned. Every scan, here every 20 ms, the controller does three things in order: it copies the state of every input point into memory, it solves every rung of the running routines from the top down, and it writes the result of every output rung to the output points. Nothing happens between scans. A sensor that flickers for 2 ms between two scans is never seen; an output written by rung 3 and overwritten by rung 9 is only ever what rung 9 said. Hold on to those two facts and most ladder mysteries dissolve.

Reading a rung

A rung is a path from the left power rail to the right. Instructions on the left (conditions) either pass power or block it; the instruction on the right (the output) does something when power reaches it. In Logix Connect you can draw the rung with the instruction toolbar or type it as text, exactly the way Studio 5000 copies a rung to the clipboard:

XIC(Start_PB)XIO(Stop_PB)OTE(Motor);

Read it left to right: examine Start_PB if closed (true when the tag is 1), examine Stop_PB if open (true when the tag is 0), output energize Motor. Instructions written one after another are in series: all must be true. A branch, instructions that can each complete the path, is written in square brackets with a comma between the legs:

The classic seal-in: Start or Motor itself, and not Stop, keeps Motor on
[XIC(Start_PB),XIC(Motor)]XIO(Stop_PB)OTE(Motor);

The editor draws it like this. This is the real one from Part IV’s step 1, with Stop normally closed and a batch-done condition added; the tag descriptions are printed above the contacts (View → Tag Descriptions in Ladder).

That rung is the most important one in the book. Press Start: the upper leg is true, the output comes on. Release Start: the lower leg, XIC(Line_Run), is now true because the output is on, so the rung stays true: the output seals itself in. Press Stop: the stop contact goes false, the output drops, and both legs are now false. Every Run bit on every machine you will ever program is this rung.

Entering rungs

There are two ways in, and you can mix them. Graphically: drag an instruction from the instruction toolbar onto a rung; blue drop zones appear between instructions and at the ends of each branch leg, and the (End) rung accepts a drop too and starts a new rung. A new instruction opens with its ? operand in an edit box and the tag browser under it, filtered to tags that fit: type a name or a number, pick from the list, press Enter. A name that does not exist yet is created as a new tag (and aliased by itself if it matches a wired point, chapter 5). Drag [ , ] onto a slot for an empty two-leg branch, or onto an instruction to branch around it; the + at the bottom of a branch adds a leg.

As text: double-click a rung (or select it and press Enter) to edit it as neutral text, the same text Logix Designer shows when you edit a rung as ASCII. Rung on the toolbar (or Ins) adds an empty rung after the selected one. Enter accepts, Esc cancels, and the rung draws itself as you type.

To change one instruction for a relative, select it: the change to bar under it offers the others of its family (XIC and XIO; OTE, OTL and OTU; TON, TOF and RTO; CTU and CTD; the compares; the math), and the operands stay. Right-click gives the same choices. A branch can go without what is on it: select it by its left bar and choose Remove branch, keep instructions. Click a leg’s wire to select that leg alone; Delete leg takes the leg and what is on it. Comment (Ctrl+D) puts a note above the rung; use it, the lessons in Part IV comment every rung and you should too. Delete Rung and Move Rung Up / Down (Ctrl+↑ / Ctrl+↓) reorder. The semicolon at the end is the rung terminator; the editor adds it if you forget.

Try it

Enter [XIC(Start_PB),XIC(Motor)]XIO(Stop_PB)OTE(Motor);. Click the OTE and choose OTL on the change-to bar, then click the lower leg’s wire and press Del: the rung reads XIC(Start_PB)XIO(Stop_PB)OTL(Motor);. Ctrl+Z twice brings the seal-in back. Now select the branch by its left bar and choose Remove branch, keep instructions: both contacts stay, in series, and the rung needs Start and Motor to turn Motor on, so it never will.

Logic → Verify Routine (or Verify on the toolbar) checks every rung: unknown tags, wrong parameter counts, a tag used as the wrong type. Errors appear in the Errors pane with the rung number. A routine that does not verify does not run.

Rung text: the syntax on one page

Keep this open while you type. The editor accepts exactly what Studio 5000 puts on the clipboard when you copy a rung, so everything here transfers.

You wantYou typeNotes
an instructionXIC(Start)mnemonic in capitals, parameters in brackets, no spaces needed
instructions in series (AND)XIC(A)XIC(B)OTE(C);one after another; all must be true
a branch (OR)[XIC(A),XIC(B)]OTE(C);square brackets around the legs, a comma between legs
a leg with several instructions[XIC(A)XIC(B),XIC(C)]OTE(D);A and B, or C
a branch inside a branch[XIC(A)[XIC(B),XIC(C)],XIC(D)]OTE(E);nest as deep as you need; count your brackets
two outputs on one rungXIC(A)[OTE(B),OTE(C)];an output branch: both energized together
a bit of a wordXIC(Word.3) XIC(Exist[0].12)dot, then the bit number
a member of a structureXIC(Dwell.DN) GEQ(Dwell.ACC,500)timers: .PRE .ACC .EN .TT .DN; counters: .CU .CD .DN; control: .DN .UL .POS .LEN
an array elementMOV(Vals[2],Out)index in square brackets; a tag used as the index is fine
a numberGEQ(Count,20) TON(T1,1500,0)plain digits; a decimal point makes it REAL; 16#FF and 2#1010 work
a timer / counterTON(Dwell,1000,0) CTU(Boxes,10,0)tag, preset, accumulator (start value)
a shift registerBSL(Exist[0],Exist_Ctl,LS1,48)array, CONTROL tag, source bit, length
a routine callJSR(S1_Run)the routine runs at this point in the scan, then the scan comes back
the end of the rung;the editor adds it if you forget
The mistakes everyone makes once

Unbalanced brackets. Every [ needs a ], every ( a ). The Errors pane says where.

A space in a tag name. Start PB is two things; Start_PB is one.

The same tag on two OTEs. Only the last one in the scan counts. Use a branch on one rung, or OTL and OTU.

An ONS without its own storage bit. ONS(X_ONS) needs a BOOL used nowhere else; two one-shots sharing a bit both fail.

Reading the done bit of a timer that never resets. A TON resets when its rung goes false; if the rung is always true, .DN comes on once and stays.

Forgetting the JSR. A routine nobody calls does nothing (chapter 9).

Online

Switch to Run mode and the ladder is online: contacts, coils and wires turn green with power flow, and timers and counters show their accumulators. Anything that was on since the last redraw is drawn, so a one-scan pulse is a visible blink. View → Highlight Power Flow shades the whole energized path, which Logix does not do but a beginner finds useful.

In Program mode an edit takes effect at once. While the controller runs, a change to a rung does not: it becomes an edit zone that you take through the same steps as in Logix Designer, and the original rung keeps running until you say otherwise. The Online edits buttons appear on the toolbar while the controller runs.

StepCommandMarginWhat the controller runs
1Start Pending Rung Edit, or simply change the rungi above rThe original (r). The i rung exists only in the editor.
2Accept Pending Rung / Program EditsI above RStill the original. The edit is now in the controller. A rung with an error is not accepted.
3Test Accepted Program Edits (again to Untest)I above RThe edit (I). The original (R) is skipped and drawn faded.
4Assemble Accepted Program EditsnoneThe edit, permanently. The original is removed.

Finalize All Edits in Program accepts and assembles in one step; Cancel throws pending or accepted edits away. A rung you did not touch keeps its one-shot and counter edge memory through an edit, so editing one rung does not re-fire another. Tag values carry over an edit; only Reset Sim or Tools → Clear Tag Values zero them.

Try it

In an empty project place a Push Button, a second Push Button with NC ticked (its signal is then 1 until pressed, like a real stop button) and an Indicator Light. Name them Start_PB, Stop_PB and Lamp; their signals alias themselves as Start_PB_Pressed, Stop_PB_Pressed and Lamp_On (chapter 5). Write [XIC(Start_PB_Pressed),XIC(Lamp_On)]XIC(Stop_PB_Pressed)OTE(Lamp_On);, go to Run mode and press the buttons. Then untick NC on the stop button: the lamp will not light at all, because a released NO button reads 0. That is why the stop is wired normally closed and read with XIC: a broken wire reads the same as a pressed stop, and the machine stops.
